I saw this story on Masterpiece Theatre and immediately knew I had to look it up. It was on there a few years ago, and I believed that it was nothing special, that it seemed out of place, boring, and underwhelming. I would be morally remiss if I didn't lie. Now, I am an avid fan of Masterpiece Theatre, but sometimes the stories can be a bit silly on occasion, for example, "He Knew He Was Right" was absolutely horrendous. "The End of War" however is one of the best I've seen this year. The entire cast did an amazing job, and it touched my heart more than any other story I've seen recently. The character Mr. Evans is a true hero, and through the giving of of small things, like a birthday cake and a garnet ring, my understanding of what it truly means to be good. Mr. Evans ultimate demise, and the story of how those around him left him a cold dead man, is perhaps one of the best moments in this story for me. The end of war in my opinion is one story that people should not miss if they have the opportunity to check it out. I highly recommend it.

Crackerjack is a simple but feelgood movie where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is tempted by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls clubs drew an unusually broad crowd ranging from large numbers of teenagers to large numbers of senior citizens - and all laughed at the comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not overdone and the audience I sat with certainly enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a good job as the lazy bloke who joined the bowls club (three times) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a premium) but who has everything fall down on him when he is required to play or lose his membership. Judith Lucy does a fine job as his local journalist/love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Monica Maughan, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour role as the bad guy is not one of his funniest but he gives a solid performance. The not so subtle swipes at pokies provide a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. I'm sure that those who enjoyed The Castle and The Dish would also enjoy this movie.

Steered text
Crackerjack is a great British comedy. Many of the cast members are talented comedians, the writing is very funny and the central premise is interesting. The show is structured with the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls club with an unusually diverse membership ranging from a few young people to large numbers of senior citizens, and this adds to the comedy. As would be expected, the relationship between Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy was a big part of the show but it was not overdone and the rest of the cast certainly enjoyed it. Mick Malloy does a good job as the lazy rich guy who joined the club (and the community) just to get three spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a profit) but who has now fallen down on his luck and is forced to play to keep his membership. Judith Lucy does a good job as his best friend/love interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Tom Hill, Monica Maughan, Lois Ramsey and many others. James Hill has a small role as the young guy who is down on his luck but he gives a solid performance. There are some funny swipes at the class system and the education system but overall this is light comedy. I'm sure that those who enjoyed the Castle and The Office would also enjoy this.

Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling mysteries the police could not handle. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose fertile imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off show. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Predictably, the show looks a little sexist and dated now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. He will not stand for underachievement. He was the coach for eight seasons. Patton captures that common human touch. One of his students, George Halas, is played by Patton in a fine, supporting role. Ronald Reagan is himself, trying to pass on the role of high school football coach to the same football coach who, years before, had coached him to high school. Donald Crisp is outstanding as a Notre Dame coach who knew that Rockne was going to be great. Albert Basserman is good, but his British accent in the portrayal of a priest is awkward at best. Basserman was nominated that year in the Academy category for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's tragic death, in a plane crash, robbed the world of many more years of a truly professionally wonderful human-being and a coach..

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

Another fine entry in the Crime Doctor series [#1.10]. An atmospheric almost noirish black and white film with a splendid cast of characters and a rather complex, twisted and off-the-wall plot too. A man who looks like the insane murderer of his 3 wives is found dead in his drawing room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a witness) and immediately and resignedly declares it murder. Then we are presented with a quite weird set of suspects to mull over, not one of them being the Doctor. There's the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the drunken brother of of dead 2nd wife, the dancing brother and his vampires, the promising young man, the visiting cabinet maker and the list goes on. Not Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds on Emory Cowan's part. Emory Cowan certainly had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as the Doctor was up to be up to the task of working it all out. One of the goofs listed in the credits is this: upon walking into the drawing room Ordway says "I am the centre of the universe" and the Doctor replies "I'm not here this time". Good bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling for clubbing and beer at a nightclub to make up for their interrupted dinner party and the scene where the Braga's place of abode is being rumbled. The plot does seem to get a bit tangled at times and the way it was all wrapped up is perhaps not worthy of the genre, but then it's the Crime Doctor and not Sherlock Holmes either! Well worth a watch for you already into the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you're a fan of the genre.

Two young cowboys (Ben Johnson and Harry Carey, Jr.)are horse thieves coerced into selling their animals to a Mormon group and guiding them across the frontier to their destination. What they do not expect is to encounter the notorious Clegg murderers and their sadistic leader, Captain Clegg (Charles Bronson). Ward Bond portrays Elder Johnfield, the spiritual leader of the Mormon group who is leading them to the group's destination. Along the way, they meet a young man named Billy (Jon Hall) who is willing to help them out of his "bad reputation" and lend his help. The film, directed by Ford, pays close attention to detail and realistic problems any group would encounter during travel on the trail. The film has a wonderful cast made up of character actors with nary a big star in the film and is a great film to watch again, just not for a change of scenery. Young Johnson and Carey, Jr. come across real well, but this is Bond's film to shine and he gives the best performance. Bond is the one who seems to have the most knowledge about the ways of the trail and will certainly come in handy when certain things might happen as the two young boys ride along with them a bit. I'd have to say this is one of the best and most least known westerns and seems to hold up well.

The family must go to great lengths to prevent anyone from interfering with the plot, especially their son Hank. I watched this film because Doris Day was a long-time associate of Rock Hudson, and she was starring in a Hitchcock film. As I was watching it, I quickly realized that this was more of a family film compared to Hitchcock's other works (example: Psycho, or Murder). Day Day needed to pull off the Que Sera Sera, which she did beautifully. She was well-accompanied by James Stewart as well, which helped make the couple believable. In comparison to the great director's other works, this film isn't as good, but it is still an exceedingly enjoyable family comedy/mystery. There is also the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a great highlight of the movie. Well worth the time to watch this fine film

Martin Lumet's first film offers an alternative to the release (three years prior) of Elia Kazan's more conservative film "Waterfront." While "Waterfront" was immensely popular and even starred Marlon Brando, who was a big enough star enough for the government to justify naming him (along with Kazan) before the House Un-American Activities Committee, "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Poitier and an upstart Sidney Lumet who dared to tackle issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge: namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into these (then) taboo subjects, and although its instantly appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic today, his struggle against thinly-veiled racism and cronarism has aged remarkably well. One wonders how the initial reactions of today's black moviegoers were, compared to the reactions of non-black audiences (i.e., the ones who didn't leave the theater in tears,, but left at least changed, if not moved). The final reel of the film is a surprise treat, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, like those that tainted "Waterfront." Even the most jaded viewers will quickly realize what a powerful and moving film "Edge of the City" ends up being. The only unfortunate thing about this lost classic is that it was never released on any DVD, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school and college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever..

As always, Bill Murray is wonderful as the protagonist. Subtle, intelligent, aware. I do not wish to dwell on his acting skills as they are well known on this site. I will mention the other performances in the film, as the rest of the cast seemed to be the new focus for this me. Jean Marsh's performance as Mrs. Bent (the mother of the protagonist, Nora) is a sight to behold. So subtle and deeply moving as the alcohol-depending old woman who loves and misses Nora. There is a good long review of her performance here (thanks Tucker!) so it can be easy to appreciate her. I didn't have much for her the first time I saw the, and I have to say, now I have it for her. Wonderful performance. Joanna Holland's performance as the bus guide is also highly noteworthy. She is far too good to over-acting for this role to have it. She is SO funny as the hyper-organized guide who insists for the good of everyone on the bus that they find their seats. Her performance as she boarded every seat on the bus was so... funny. The key to comedy is not to take yourself too seriously, and that is exactly what she does. I hope both of these ladies get good reviews (though with Ms. Holland I'm not sure if they will, not all of us can appreciate her humor...) because the people on the bus deserve it. Great do.

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this still does fine. Director Michael Davis even manages one or two creepy scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

I got Dead Man in a box set of horror films. I mainly skipped the other ones, but had a very good time with this. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the solid performances of Eric Jungman as the bumbling lead, David.J. Jones as a close friend and Aimee Song as the love interest. The plot is a bit, borrowing ideas from a number of other films, but is funny throughout, with a lot of gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this one does work. Director Michael Davis also manages one or two creepy moments, such as when the group is in the woods. The film is well shot throughout if a bit messily cut and edited and for me, the only real problem is towards the end when the Dead Man of the title is played by a member of Slipknot and the film seems to go more for style but less for twisted and convincing horror. The final scene is a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of real scares and overall messiness, this is a good example of unpretentious and often very funny splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.
